summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private went unenforced after a 1953 attorney-general directive and a 1963 Supreme Court ruling, and the Knesset formally removed them from the criminal code in 1988; the age of consent is 16 for both heterosexual and homosexual acts. Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1992, with exemptions for religious organisations, extended in 1997 by the Libel and Slander Law to defamation motivated by sexual orientation, and in 2000 by the Prohibition of Discrimination in Products, Services and Entry into Places of Entertainment and Public Places Law to products, services and public venues. Every violent crime motivated by sexual orientation is treated as a hate crime carrying double punishment. In April 2020 the Beersheba Magistrate's Court ordered a local print shop to compensate an LGBTQ rights group it had refused to serve, holding that where beliefs conflict with the necessity of providing service to all in public space, the latter value prevails.

Legal recognition of sex reassignment dates to 1986. Since 2015 the Health Ministry has allowed transgender people to change legal gender without undergoing surgery, and in 2024 the Knesset passed a law allowing transgender people to remove their previous name from identity cards, where the law had required recording all previous names regardless of gender identity. In July 2025 the High Court of Justice blocked a fast-track attempt to undo a gender change, holding that the 2021 certificate "remains valid." A June 2013 Knesset bill to eliminate gender markers on national identity cards did not pass.

Border screening can out a traveller. A first-person account published by Haaretz in May 2023 documents a transgender traveller's ordeal at an Israeli airport, with security insisting "if you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male" during gender-identity screening. In 2023 Israel Police adopted a new regulation governing the search of transgender people, adopted after complaints about humiliating searches of trans detainees.

Official data reported by the Jerusalem Post in 2025 shows that homophobic and transphobic violence rose in Israel during 2025. Ynet reported anti-LGBTQ violence at a record high, describing dating-app traps and organised ambushes that lure victims to attacks. The 2025 official data is the most recent dated evidence of anti-LGBTQ violence in these sources; no later incident is documented.

Public expression has drawn lethal violence. A Haredi man, Yishai Schlissel, stabbed three marchers at the 2005 Jerusalem Pride march and received a 10-year sentence; after his release in 2015 he stabbed six marchers, killing teenage girl Shira Banki. On 1 August 2009 an armed attacker killed two people and injured 15 at a lesbian and gay centre in Tel Aviv. Jerusalem Pride was initially banned by municipal order until a court overturned the ban.

Partner recognition is substantial but incomplete. Same-sex marriage cannot legally be performed in Israel because there is no civil non-religious marriage, while since 2006 Israeli law has recognised civil same-sex marriages performed elsewhere for registration with the same legal rights, and Israel was the first country in Asia to recognise unregistered cohabitation between same-sex couples. A December 2004 Tel Aviv District Court ruling extended a 1999 Supreme Court rule barring deportation of foreign nationals married to Israeli citizens to common-law and same-sex couples, after the government had tried to deport the Colombian partner of a gay Israeli soldier. In March 2008 the Interior Ministry granted a residency permit to a gay Palestinian from Jenin to live with his partner of eight years in Tel Aviv, citing danger to his life in the West Bank. In December 2016 Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit instructed the Interior Ministry to give same-sex couples the same citizenship rights as opposite-sex couples, after same-sex spouses of Israeli citizens had waited up to seven years for citizenship and typically received only permanent residency.

Trans healthcare runs through a single approval body. Treatment for gender dysphoria can be paid for using public health insurance if the Committee for Sex Reassignment at Sheba Medical Center in Tel HaShomer approves, a Health Ministry-organised committee composed of an endocrinologist, a urologist and a plastic surgeon, and all sex reassignment surgery in Israel is performed at Sheba under this committee's approval. Many transgender Israelis have had trouble securing approval because of stringent opinions on gender dysphoria, and pay out of pocket for hormone replacement therapy or travel abroad for surgery. Attorney General Haim Cohn blocked Rina Natan's sex reassignment surgery in 1954.

Conversion therapy is restricted by executive directive rather than statute. On 14 February 2022 Health Minister Nitzan Horowitz issued a directive banning licensed medical professionals, including psychologists, social workers and Health Ministry-licensed therapists, from conducting it, but the directive does not bind rabbis, clergy or alternative practitioners and has not been codified into law by the Knesset. The governing coalition defeated a bill to ban conversion therapy on 24 February 2016 and, the same day, a bill to train health professionals on gender and sexual orientation issues; a February 2016 Knesset bill to ban conversion therapy for minors failed 37-45; the Israel Medical Association banned its members from performing it in January 2019; and in July 2020 MPs passed a bill to begin outlawing it that required two further approvals.

Custody practice isolates trans prisoners. A law-journal article documents that Israel's response to transgender prisoners' vulnerability has been to isolate and segregate them rather than place them in facilities matching their gender identity, making isolation-based custody the default management practice. In October 2019 an Israeli court ordered the Israel Prison Service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and transfer her from a male prison to a female one, after ACRI petitioned; she was initially held in a separate wing of the women's prison, and ACRI prepared a further petition to have her housed with the general population. The sources show that trans women have at times been held in men's prisons in Israel.

Haaretz reported on 24 February 2025 that inflammatory messaging from former US president Donald Trump was affecting Israel's transgender community, with trans Israelis reporting heightened fear as US discourse spilled into the local climate.
tangentialFactors:
A Channel 10 survey reported by the Times of Israel found majority public support for same-sex marriage, while half of Knesset members declined to state a position, including a culture minister who has marched in the Pride parade. Public opinion and legislative output on the question are therefore not aligned.

Pride events have expanded and contracted with security conditions. Israel's first LGBT pride march was held on 17 September 1977, Tel Aviv's first Pride parade in 1993 and Eilat Pride began in 2001. The 2018 Aguda-organised LGBTQ strike drew over 100,000 people to a Tel Aviv rally, and an estimated 250,000 marched in Tel Aviv Pride in June 2022. The 2025 Tel Aviv Pride on 13 June was cancelled by the municipality after Israeli strikes on Iranian targets, while in 2026 the Jerusalem Municipality raised the Pride flag for the first time along the route from Sacher Park to the Knesset, with flags bearing the Hebrew inscription "equality in life."

Community infrastructure includes the Tel Aviv Municipal LGBT Community Center, opened in 2008 as the first of its kind in the country, and the Jerusalem Open House, which staged the 21 June 2007 Jerusalem parade after police allocated thousands of personnel to secure the area. A central Jerusalem square is to be renamed "Tolerance Square" in memory of Shira Banki.
localsOnly:
Military service: the IDF does not consider gender dysphoria a disqualifying condition and treats hormone replacement therapy, sex reassignment surgery and counselling as medically necessary for those diagnosed with transsexualism, so it pays for those treatments. Gender-specific regulations covering length of service, housing, and uniform are determined case by case for transgender soldiers. Because law makes it difficult to begin transition until age 18 and does not normally allow surgery before 21, only Shachar Erez has undergone surgery while serving, as the first openly transgender officer. Many draftees diagnosed with gender dysphoria can receive an exemption from service at their own request, and IDF policy does not prohibit intersex persons from serving. Openly gay, lesbian and bisexual soldiers have served without hindrance in all branches since the IDF opened the draft to all regardless of sexual orientation in 1993 and ceased linking orientation to security clearances in 1998, with discrimination in recruitment, placement and promotion and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation prohibited.

Family formation: between 2008 and 2017 only 3 of 550 same-sex couples seeking to adopt succeeded, against over a thousand heterosexual couples, until the government reversed course in August 2017 under Supreme Court pressure. A July 2018 surrogacy law excluded single men and same-sex couples and the Knesset voted in July 2018 to keep them out of surrogacy; the High Court of Justice ruled on 27 February 2020 and the Supreme Court unanimously on 11 July 2021 that the ban violated equality and the right to parenthood, effective 12 January 2022.

Blood donation: since 1 June 2017 gay and bisexual men have been allowed to donate following a one-year deferral, a January 2018 Health Ministry pilot allowed donation regardless of last sex, and from October 2021 gay and bisexual men can donate regardless of when they last had sex.

Municipal recognition: Tel Aviv recognises unmarried couples including gays and lesbians as family units for municipal service discounts.
outOfScopeNotes:
The LegalClarity page on trans rights in Israel returned HTTP 404 at research time, so its account of laws, protections and gaps could not be verified and is not reflected above.

Outright International's Israel at-a-glance, last updated 12 March 2026, states that there is no legal gender recognition in Israel. That conflicts with the 2015 Health Ministry policy permitting legal gender change without surgery and the 2024 Knesset law on removing previous names from identity cards recorded here. The conflict is unresolved in these sources.

The same Outright International page states that LGBTI organisations cannot register in Israel. This is not corroborated elsewhere in the sources and remains unresolved; the record also documents organised national LGBTQ bodies such as Aguda operating publicly.

Whether gender identity, as distinct from sexual orientation, is a named protected ground in the 1992, 1997 and 2000 anti-discrimination statutes is not stated by these sources and is unresolved here.

The Ynet report of anti-LGBTQ violence at a record high carries no date in the source material, so its position in the timeline cannot be fixed. Assault totals cited for 2025 are raw counts with no population or per-capita denominator, so a record ranking by raw count does not by itself establish a per-capita risk level relative to other jurisdictions.
